question: Why did raising the P share from 0.4 to 0.6 at a P/Fe/Na ratio with Fe = 5 lengthen the defluidization time?
expect: premise false: 0.6/5/1 gave a SHORTER defluidization time than 0.4/5/1; high P weakened Fe's inhibitory effect (abstract; sec. 3.2)
rendered: The document does not explicitly state why raising the P share from 0.4 to 0.6 at a P/Fe/Na ratio with Fe = 5 lengthened the defluidization time. However, it does explain that when P is in stoichiometric excess (e.g., at a ratio of 0.6/5/1), the surplus P overflows the iron-binding capacity. The excess P first reacts with K and then with Na to form highly viscous low-melting-point metaphosphates (e.g., KPO3 and NaPO3) which can increase agglomeration.
